utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Tuesday, August 18, 2009. I welcome everyone, Mr. Praljak first. I also welcome our accused, the Defence counsels, all the representatives of the OTP, and all those helping us in this courtroom. We're a bit late because of a computer problem, but we'll now resume with our hearing and I will give the floor to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, yesterday, when we finished, we were talking about Exhibit 3D00482 and I want to continue with just a few last questions on that exhibit. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if you recall, these are the minutes of the meeting in which you participated on the 13th of January, 1993, with members of the French Army delegation that came to visit with you and others of the Croatian Army in Zagreb, and on -- yesterday we were talking about the text on the second page of the English version in which you -- your position is reported, and I'll read your words or the words that are attributed to you: "The Croatian position has been clear from the very beginning. The territory that belongs to the Croats matches the borders of the Banovina Hrvatska from the 1939 division of Yugoslavia synchronised with the 1981 census --" I'm sorry, "... synchronised with the 1981 census. The 1991 census is not valid." General, just a few questions on the census issue that you refer to here. Would you agree with me that if one were to have relied on the 1981 census figures, that that would have resulted in a greater proportion of Croat persons living in the territories that had been a part of the Banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few more Croats in the 1981 census than in the 1991 census, that is correct. That difference is not great. The 1991 census was simply not completed, according to the law, although it is still seen as 3 authoritative. In other words, because of the war, a final assessment of that census was never made by the competent authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think you answered my question, and actually I think we're in agreement that there would be some difference as between 1981 and 1991, but perhaps it would not be a hugely significant difference. But let's take this opportunity to look at a few of the numbers on this, because I want to try to flesh out what you're saying here, in terms of how the territory would be synchronised with the census figures for 1981. Were you telling the French delegation there that territory from the Banovina would be abandoned or given up if it were found to be a territory that did not contain a sufficient number of Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I didn't quite understand your question. What do you mean, abandoned, an abandoned territory? Could you please define in?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, here you say that territory belonging to the Croats matches the borders of the Banovina Hrvatska, synchronised with the 1981 census. Now, my understanding of that is that you start with the borders of the former Banovina and that there would be an adjustment of those borders based upon the relative populations as they existed in 1981. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state my position clearly and precisely, starting with the initial thoughts I had when Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised, and starting with the initial Cutileiro plan. Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a condition for the referendum, should have comprised three constituent bodies, and the relative proportion of inhabitants should be honoured by such principles. One of such constituent units was supposed to be the unit in which Croats were in absolute or relative majority. This was supposed to be based on the 1981 census, although as I said, that is not completely correct either, given that many Croats who emigrated did not respond to that census. Such census, truth be said, is not fully valid either, but that was precisely because Croats kept moving out and their numbers dwindled in Bosnia-Herzegovina, irrespective of the fact that in 1939, when the government in Belgrade was forced to recognise the Croatian issue in the then Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off, but you're moving a little bit beyond the territory that I'm trying to keep us in, in terms of this discussion that you're having with the French. Maybe the best way to do this is to look at some of the numbers. In your binder, toward the end, you should be able to find Exhibit P10519, and this is a collection of the census data from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes, you've got it there. Keep going. That's right. And you'll see that what this has is the census data for all the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina for three decades; 1971, 1981, 1991. So it gives us an opportunity to discuss the numbers that you're referring to with the French. Let's look at Stolac in the census because Stolac is a place that, whether you're talking about 1981 or 1991, had a relative majority of Muslim people living there. Now, we also know - I don't think there's disagreement - that Stolac falls within the territory that used to be part of the Banovina from 1939, and of course Stolac also falls in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So now I just want to make sure. When you're telling the French that the territory of the Croats matches the Banovina synchronised with the 1981 census, you're not telling them that the Croats were prepared to abandon Stolac, simply because that was an area in 1981 that did not contain a relative majority or an absolute majority of Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only partially, Mr. Stringer. Stolac was an administrative unit, a municipality, to which some villages were annexed so as to -- well, you can see the figures of Croatian population dwindling from one year to the next in order to arrive at a Muslim majority. The municipality of Stolac, as a banovina municipality in 1939, is no longer the same, Stolac municipality, as the one formed in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was done to regulate the percentages of population in several municipalities. But you see, see the difference between 7041 Croats and 7113 Muslims in 1971 was not all that significant. For the municipality of Capljina, three villages were supposed to be annexed to the Stolac municipality to have a relative majority of Croats, but no one talked about ethnically-pure areas. Sarajevo was 24 per cent Croats 30 years ago, in Zenica 30.000, but none of the units or cantons were envisaged as ethnically pure but something that would be approximate to satisfy the principle of some sort of balance between all of the three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, and then, of course, within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna -- and in your binder you should be able to find the map which may be of assistance to us, P09276, which is, I believe, just behind the census, that's the map that was prepared that shows the borders both of the HZ-HB and also the Banovina from 1939, I mean if you look right in the middle of all of it, you see the municipality of Jablanica, which, of course, has always been a very high absolute majority of Muslim population, so there's really no way, is there, to synchronise the Croat territory with the 1981 census or the 1991 census in the way that you're proposing to the French delegation, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, Mr. Stringer. That is simply incorrect. For the municipality of Jablanica, that is so, but it also goes for Jajce, which throughout history had a Croat majority, but at this point in time it was no longer so. Herceg-Bosna that you are talking about is not what I am talking about. "Herceg-Bosna" is a term, as you could see -- well, at least half of the HVO soldiers were not under command of the headquarters of the HVO. The Zenica Brigade was formed, the Bihac and other units were formed, in order to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let us not mix apples and pears. This was based on the propositions put by the international community by which ethnically-pure areas were not envisaged. Kakanj, as well as Vares, used to be territories with a significant Croat majority, and here they were merely units -- administrative units in which Croats would be one of the constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This changed throughout the negotiations. A number of Muslims and Serbs lived --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is that what you are proposing to the French as being the position of the Croats is something that was completely unworkable because, in fact, throughout the area of what used to be the Banovina, you have Muslims, Croats and, of course, Serbs as well living, and the majorities and the locations and the concentrations of the different peoples is highly mixed throughout the Banovina area, and there's really no way, is there, to synchronise territory with the demographic situation that prevailed either in 1981 or 1991, at least not without moving people; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, no one asked for any people to be moved or an ethnically-pure territory. I have a question for you. Why don't you bring here those who drafted the Dayton Accords, because I find it a much worse solution, much less logical solution, than the one I am representing? Dayton split that country in a far worse manner than this principle would have. Do bring in the American president and his men who drafted that to answer those questions. My thinking was logical, along the lines of how to organise a state respecting civic and genealogical principles, and I still stand by that no matter what you think. There were no ethnically-pure areas foreseen. There were only majorities which, based on the principle of reciprocity, could function at the best possible -- in the best possible way, the way it is regulated in Switzerland. There are cantons there housing three peoples, and they have a good life. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry to cut you off, but you've expressed your views about Switzerland already and what I'd like to do is keep this moving to the next document, unless there are more questions about this one from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I looked at this document very closely, as I look at all documents very closely, but notably this one. Now, contrary to what the Prosecutor is saying, this is not a meeting with the French Army. This is a very high-level meeting in France, because there's a number of ministries involved. We have the French ambassador, so it's France, actually, that is meeting up with you. So I'd like to know, as far as you know, whether this delegation also met President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. As you know, two days later I went back to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am not familiar whether they met up with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the document, we see in brackets that the 1991 census is not valid. That's in brackets, and it seems that this is something you uttered. So why wouldn't this census have been valid, according to you? I'm putting this question to you because in all trials we've had in this Tribunal, this census -- this 1991 census is used as a reference, and you're saying it's not valid. Could you please explain why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is legal regulation in place for a census to be declared valid. The final act in such a process of conducting a census is the adoption of such a census by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This never happened. Legally speaking, that process is never completed, irrespective of the fact that it is widely used here. That's one thing. Another thing, Your Honour. The beginning of the war in Croatia had already taken place. A great many Croats in Germany, Switzerland, and elsewhere did not attend the census. They did not provide their data, because people were simply afraid to go back. Given that the Croats are the smallest nation in terms of numbers, although in terms of immigration they have the greatest figures among the three, it is a very sensitive issue. Imagine that all the Croats abroad responded to the census. That is why this 1991 census is not fully true and is not valid, and I believe this Tribunal should not take it as such unless this is only by way of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I understand what you said. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P01788. The last document was from January of 1993. We're going to move forward now to April of 1993. And for the record, Mr. President, you'll note that the English translation for some reason does not contain the date, but the date is found in the original language version, the 2nd of April, 1993. General, these are minutes from a meeting of commanders of brigades and special-purpose units from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. You'll there see at the top that it has you present, together with Mr. Kordic, Mr. Kostroman, Tihomir Blaskic, and also Mr. Coric. Do you remember being present at this meeting that was chaired by you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present at the meeting, but I did not chair it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, because it says right under the names that the meeting was chaired by you; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says so, but I only provided explanations during that meeting. I don't remember chairing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is all that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we agree that at this period of time, you were a major general of the Croatian Army and, in that sense, were the highest-ranking person among those present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a major general of the Croatian Army, but although it says here that I was a general for them, I was Slobodan Praljak who came from Croatia, as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to explain my view of the situation and the way I thought the authorities stood on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me put it to you, General, that in fact you were also an assistant minister of defence for Croatia and that your role there was to act as an interlocutory person whose presence -- you were coming with a high level, a high position, and that you were there to inform all of these people what the positions and the policies of the Croatian government were in respect of the events that are being discussed here. Isn't that the main reason why you were there is to inform them of the policies and the developments coming from the highest level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite so, not quite. I went there once the Vance-Owen Plan was signed. I was what I was, that is correct, and people -- the people there knew it was so. However, much was said on my own initiative, and I asked for initiative from Mr. Izetbegovic. If you recall, I waited in Mostar for him to send two prominent Bosniaks, Muslims, for us to go to Central Bosnia, which in a way represented a political challenge, so that we could discuss with the people there, tell them that the plan had been signed, and what things needed to be done to end the war and come up with a peaceful solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, my wait in Mostar was in vain. Therefore, I set off with some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move to the second paragraph on the first page, where -- well, just for background here, I think we're talking about the meeting opens and you inform those present about the arrival of five or six commissioned officers from Herzegovina. You report on the signing of the plan, which I take to be the Vance-Owen Plan, and you continue your briefing, if I can call it that. And moving to the second paragraph, you say: "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic's option, is finally out of the question. He has signed. "The international community wanted two of the sides involved to agree so that the third side would be under greater pressure. The Serbian side will hardly be able to resist the pressure, but they will have to sign." Now, that turned out to be incorrect, didn't it? In fact, the Serbs never signed Vance-Owen, and the plan itself never came to pass; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says that the international community insisted that they reach an agreement, that is to say, the Bosnian -- Bosniak and Croatian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that they then will exert pressure upon the Serbs for them to sign too. Unfortunately, they didn't have enough skill or goodwill or interest or force to persuade the Serbs to sign the plan, and they did not. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so as a result, then, the plan never came into existence, did it, because the three -- not all three parties to the plan agreed to it; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that all three sides did not sign the plan, but that still did not mean that two sides, which had signed the plan, should not stand by the principles elaborated in the plan, and that remaining true to the principles and the general agreement reached, that they should not act together and force the third side, in the military and political sense, to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now that -- continuing down a few lines, you say: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna will remain. It will have its own assembly and the provincial government will rule the country. The central government will have nothing. The Sarajevo province will not stay the way you see it now." So what you're saying here is that the policy or the effect of Vance-Owen, from your perspective, is that now this so-called temporary body, the HZ-HB, or a temporary executive authority that was running it, which was the HVO, would, in fact, now remain in place permanently and would rule the country, the country being the Vance-Owen territory that you're referring to, isn't that true, and that the central government would have no role to play in that territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quote the Vance-Owen Plan quite exactly, with all the cantons that were established according to that plan or that should be established, and most of the functions of the state were transferred to them. Of course, the central power and authority was -- well, it remained. It was the army, Foreign Affairs and so on. But everything else to do with the daily life and running of the country would be located in the cantons, who had power and authority comparable to the population in the canton itself. And that was precisely set out there and signed by Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Boban, and all the others who attended those negotiations. So the plan was signed by the representatives of the two nations from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was no reason to leave it behind, as Mr. Izetbegovic did immediately afterwards, meddling with the plan and so on and so forth without any actual desire to see it take effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on the next page of your version, General, you continue, saying that there would only be 1 per cent of Croats left in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina due to moving out and population of the Muslims and Serbs: "Salvation lies in protecting the population and enhancing the birth-rate." You say: "Our population outside these provinces will have a hard life. The Muslims are not aware of their losses." Now, General, when you say that "our population," meaning the Croat population, "outside of these provinces will have a hard life," isn't the message there that Croats who are living outside of this Croatian area you're referring to should move into the Croatian area that you're referring to because it's going to be difficult for them to live outside that area within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. You must bear in mind the fact that I am a professor of sociology, dealing with questions of migration and so on and so forth from ancient times, and I know how certain political solutions, as a general rule, result in population migration either towards North America, South America, whether we're dealing with the Aztecs, or the Indians, or the Aborigines or whatever. Or the Germans, indeed after World War II, there are patterns. If you do something poorly, then migrations necessarily arise, and this is how Yugoslavia was set up and how the Croats left. The Ottoman Empire was established in that way, the Croats left. And the way in which Bosnia-Herzegovina has been established, it is the weakest nation that is disappearing, so people who bring bad political solutions, this results in that kind of consequence. So I have a lot of knowledge in that area, and I'd like to propose that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So your political solution, General, then, is to create this Croat area where Croats living outside are going to have a hard life, and the Croats living inside are going to have a nice life, and therefore the Croats outside should come live in the Croat area that you're talking about; isn't that the political solution that you're proposing, everybody live in a separate place, and move, if it's necessary, to achieve that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It doesn't say that anywhere, and I didn't say that anywhere. All I said was that a solution of this kind would --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off. Let's continue with the document. I put it to you; you disagreed with me. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask a question. What strikes me here, Mr. Praljak, is that you seem -- you speak of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this seems to refer to that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina which does not include Herceg-Bosna; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is right, I'm talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a large portion of the Croatian people who would stay on either in cantons with the Serbian or Bosniak majority, and precisely this proportionate ratio will enable the protection of one and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It just struck me, and I raise it because it is not very easy to reconcile with what you told us yesterday, that Bosnia and Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna were identical, practically, or used for the same term. Here, it seems quite clear that there is an enormous difference. It's "either/or" in your use of the language in this sentence, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, you misunderstood me. Here -- no, I didn't put it that way yesterday. I don't know what the interpretation was. But in the books in which Franjo -- the books written by Franjo Tudjman and the history books, very often Herceg-Bosna and Bosnia-Herzegovina mean the same, they're tantamount to the same, but that is not correct in this case. Here, "Herceg-Bosna" is understood as a political/military organisation on the territory of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was inhabited by Croats and which was set up as a defence alliance. Now, in history books very often the two terms do mean the same, but in addition to this, Herceg-Bosna here is conceived differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not want to proceed in that direction. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, continuing on with this document, you're talking about -- this is page 52 in the English at the top. Are you talking about, again, Croats who would be coming from outside this Croat area, and you say: "All those who came will be refugees. Croats will be able to come to their own provinces from wherever they want and in whichever way they want. The Muslim provinces will be over-populated. Religious fanaticism will emerge in them, that is inevitable. There will be moving out and resettlement, and the population will homogenise." Then you go on to talk about de-militarisation if the Serbs sign the agreement. I'm going to skip down a few lines. You say: "Talks with the BH Army in Sarajevo are about to begin. We shall ask for HVO government in our provinces. Those who choose not to submit to that can leave our territories." So again, General, you're laying out for all of these people in Central Bosnia, on the 2nd of April, 1993, the official interpretation -- the official policy of Croat -- the Croatian people, or at least those whom you're speaking for, in respect of how Vance-Owen is going to be implemented on the ground, and that's going to mean resettlement, homogenisation of populations, a bad life for Croats who don't live in the Croatian province, and HVO government which you either take it or leave it; is that your view? Isn't that true, General? Isn't that the official interpretation of what Vance-Owen was going to mean on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer, you've got that quite wrong and you don't understand the situation. You think that certain political will can solve all political problems in the field. I'm speaking here as a scholar, and everything I said here, absolutely everything, is actually coming to pass in Bosnia-Herzegovina today. A few days ago in Zenica, for example, there were 30 marriages conducted according to Sharia law of the refugees coming from Libya. You have 210.000 fewer Croats in the Republika Srpska that was set up in Dayton. So this is history, this is history, and this is what is going to happen --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you say you're speaking as a scholar, but in fact you're speaking to these military personnel in the heart of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April, just before the conflict starts viciously between the Muslims and the Croats on the 16th of April in Central Bosnia. You're not talking as a scholar to these military personnel. You're speaking to them as an assistant minister of defence for Croatia and a major general of the Croatian Army, and you're laying out the vision -- the official vision and the policy on implementation of Vance-Owen. That's what this is about, isn't it? You're not there to give a scholarly talk to some academics.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would a scholarly talk have to be a talk to professors, to academics? I am foreseeing events, and in fact the events happened as I foresaw them. And those who foresaw that events would come to pass according to the wish in Dayton have no idea what "nations" mean and they couldn't care less. So everything I foresaw did take place, along with support from the international community, and if this is wrong, then you've got the wrong people sitting in the chair here. This is what I think is going to happen. That's what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about what really happened, not a couple of years later in Dayton and not what's happening today. Let's talk about what happened two weeks after this meeting, when the conflict was launched in Central Bosnia, the massacre occurred in Ahmici. Hundreds of Muslims throughout Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, were rounded up and arrested by HVO, held in Kaonik Prison and elsewhere. You know all about that, and that all happened because the Muslims and the ABiH did not accept this Vance -- this interpretation of Vance-Owen that you were passing on to your subordinates in Central Bosnia. Isn't that the fact of what really happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is an interpretation of -- this interpretation of the Vance-Owen plan is very precise and correct, and my interpretation has nothing to do with the BH Army attack later on, sir. And this Court has, for ten years, thought that it was executed by an unarmed people, as was stated in the Blaskic case. That is just not true. It is the aggression by the BH Army that started and was launched towards the Croats and against the Croats, and everything else that happened from Vares, Kiseljak, and so on and so forth, precisely because an ethnically-pure area was what was wanted because Vance-Owen was wrongly interpreted. In the Croatian interpretation of the Vance-Owen Plan, there was no ethnic cleansing, there was just -- there were just forecasts that if a war broke out, what would happen would happen, there would be a population migration whether you liked it or not. That was a rule, general rule, and it didn't depend on Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm really sorry to interrupt you, but again and again it is my primary issue and question, and let me ask you really to slow down and to help the interpreters. Sometimes it goes also for Mr. Stringer as well, but mainly you, Mr. Praljak, is indeed speaking very fast, and it is almost impossible to follow you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Prosecutor is putting this to you. It is very important and, I think, requires accurate answers on your part, and this should be done slowly. The Prosecutor is putting to you the following idea: There is the Vance-Owen Plan which you, as assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, you are going to spell good news to the Croats in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the document we have before us shows that you attend a meeting and you discuss the Vance-Owen Plan. The Prosecutor says to you, "Mr. Praljak, you are interpreting the Vance-Owen Plan." The Prosecutor then adds that a few days after this meeting, the events in Ahmici are going to take place. Everybody is familiar with these events. According to the Prosecutor, there is a connection. In other words, you are the spokesperson for the Croats, and then the events occur. So what he is saying is important. I think this requires a precise answer on your part and a qualified answer. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, first of all, this kind of interpretation of history, whereby a benign negotiation about my projections for the future should be linked up with the events that followed, I think, would lead all the politicians that exist in the world today into the chair of the accused. I consider that to be absurd. Now, I'm not interpreting the Vance-Owen Plan fully and completely, because it was signed and it stated quite precisely how the elections were to proceed, how the assemblies were elected for the cantons, what authority they had, and everything else. All that was signed up to by the representatives of the Bosniak Muslim people and representatives of the Croatian people as well. And as far as the Croatian people are concerned, that is to say, why we needed to go there, well, that's what I asked Mr. Izetbegovic. There was a war on, there were many Muslims, following that logic, stayed on to live in the Croatian cantons, if I can call them that, and they weren't satisfied, just as a portion of the Croats from Vares or Kakanj weren't satisfied for not -- because they weren't in a Croatian canton. So you had to explain to these people that it was precisely this cantonalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which, let's say, one where the Croatian people were in the majority, that the other nations would be protected there, the Serbs and the Muslims, and that this would be -- there would be reciprocity. They would be protected if they were outside a Croatian canton. That was my basic message. And the other fact that I say is something that we know from history, that there will be people who will no longer want to live in a canton where the Serbs were in the majority if they had suffered at the hands of the Serbs. That's not my desire or will, it's just a historical fact that has been repeated again and again. History repeated itself. So I say those people who didn't want to live there could move to a canton where the Croats were in the majority. It wasn't an invitation or anything. It was just how the facts were, the facts as they were played out in Bosnia-Herzegovina with catastrophic effects. Look at Republika Srpska, for example. And there's nothing I can add there, Your Honour. I don't know what is set out here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. As far as the other issue is concerned which was put to you by the Prosecution, there is a cause-to-effect relation between this meeting and the events in Ahmici. What do you have to say to this, because this is a very serious matter? The question is a very serious one. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to say. It's an absurd absurdity, the height of absurdity. It's just pure speculation of the lowest kind of thinking about what I am saying about history and the facts, and it goes against all my rational thinking and is an insult to me, because there's talk of de-militarisation here, as they promised us UNPROFOR would be bringing in 60.000 soldiers and so on, and ultimately they would guarantee that what was signed would be put into effect. But nobody took any notice. The spiral of war started out, and it spiraled as we know. And we saw that the international community could have whatever documents signed it liked without helping to allow it to take effect. And the Serbs made their own conclusions, the Muslims made their conclusions and said they would seize from the Croats what they could not seize from the Serbs, and then they attacked us. What happened in Ahmici is not my problem, and with indignation I reject any link of this kind. I signed up to this meeting [as interpreted]. It was a logical step. Whether everything was written properly and recorded properly, I don't know, because I know what I said. Whether it was recorded properly, I don't know. I'm talking about de-militarisation and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's been a big mistake. On page 22, line 15, the general said, "I don't know how all this was written, recorded." [In English] I signed up to this meeting. [Interpretation] The translation was, "I signed up to this meeting." Could the general repeat what he said? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it very difficult to read this handwriting. It was rather illegible, and the man who wrote it down, I don't know whether he managed to catch everything I said. I know exactly what I said, and that was to implement Vance-Owen as it was signed, with some of my thoughts about what would happen in the future, what would unfortunately happen in the future. And these are rules that we see in sociology and anthropology, these laws and rules, and those who don't know the natural laws of a science cannot deal with political issues and the establishment of state seriously, because it's not true that anything that somebody thinks up will necessarily be implemented on the ground. And it is through this lack of knowledge that catastrophes of this kind took place in these negotiations and guarantees by the international community because this was all done by people who, unfortunately, do not have enough knowledge about the human society and man as an individual being. They are unaware of their fears, desires, anxieties, and so on and so forth. They have none of that knowledge. So I'm very sorry that that is the case, and I stand by every sentence that I uttered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I really believe that your monologue has been done and is enough, and so, Mr. Stringer, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to take you back to one thing you said in the past few minutes. You were talking about, if I can put it this way, your interpretation of Vance-Owen, and you said: "This cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which, let's say, one where the Croatian people were in the majority, that the other nations would be protected there, the Serbs and the Muslims, and that this would be -- there would be reciprocity." Now, that's what you're telling us now, General, but what you were saying to all of those in Central Bosnia in April of 1993 was that those who choose not to submit to that -- let me back up. You say: "We shall ask for HVO government in our provinces. Those who choose not to submit to that can leave our territories." Now, two things. First of all, the HVO is not going to protect anybody but Croats, isn't that true, in terms of ensuring democratic participation and government when it's a structure which is purely Croatian in its -- from its inception and in which there is no -- virtually no participation or opportunity for participation among other ethnicities? Secondly, it's really ridiculous to suggest that any non-Croat person would feel that the HVO would, in fact, protect his or her interest in these territories? Isn't that both true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not interpreting the Vance-Owen Plan, because it was very clear and precise, very clear and precise. I wouldn't fully rely on my words being correctly conveyed by the person taking the notes. In any case, Mr. Stringer, in the cantons there are democratic principles, in terms of the organisation of government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are again going into lengthy talks. This is a simple question that Mr. Stringer has put to you. Why don't you just answer it? You always go astray. You lead us in -- God knows where. You speak of Libyan couples and things like that that have nothing to do with this. Why don't you just look at the question and answer the question, full stop, instead of lecturing us? Please look again at the question. The question was whether, in fact, non-Croats could trust that they would be protected, that their interests would be taken into account, in Croat cantons. That's got nothing to do with interpretation of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is incorrect, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. What sort of a question is it, could they trust? Is this a judicial question? What is trust? It's a psychological category which is strictly individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Come on Mr. -- don't lecture again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Of course I will. What trust? The Vance-Owen Plan was a plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina in which democratic institutions were supposed to be elected according to the democratic principles of most other states. That was the Vance-Owen Plan signed by two parties. Here we are now carrying out a hypothesis as to whether someone could have trusted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is all very far from being a clear answer. Let's put it in another way. On what basis would a Muslim, living in an area that would be within a Croat canton, trust that Muslim minority interests or even national interests, as you like to stress, would be respected, on what basis? Where does he find any guarantee, in what text, in what declarations, does he find something that gives him assurance that he will be protected? That's how I understood the question, but I stand to be corrected, Mr. Stringer. I do not want to make a question of my own of it. I would just like these proceedings to be a bit less baroque.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question is fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a twofold answer. There were strictly-prescribed guide-lines on the election of government in the Vance-Owen Plan, as well as on the functioning of the cantons and the central government. All those questions were widely discussed and signed as part of the plan. Secondly, this question should be put to either Mr. Vance or Mr. Owen, because they drafted the plan. Croats and Bosniaks merely signed it. This was supposed to be implemented. Thirdly, psychologically speaking, the Muslims could expect such a procedure because, from Croats, both as refugees and the wounded and members of the HVO, they were always treated equally, so at these three levels one could provide an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, continuing down, I believe this is on page 45 of your version, the bottom quarter of the page in the English, it says Colonel Blaskic opened the discussion with the commanders, and then a question was asked about Vares. Do you see that? Borivoj Malbasic asked a question about Vares?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then at that point, you said: "There is no policy that can enable us to have everything. If you think there is, tell us." What's happening here is that even as early as April of 1993, there is recognition on your part that Vares is so far to the north and so far to the east that it is not going to be a territory that you'll be able to keep within this Croatian province and, in fact, did not fall within even the Croatian province that was envisioned under Vance-Owen, so essentially here is a recognition that Vares is going to have to ultimately fall outside whatever Croatian territory exists; isn't that -- isn't that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a bit strange. Mr. Stringer, the Vance-Owen Plan was drafted by Vance, Owen, and the international community. Under that plan, Vares was not in those territories conditionally termed "Croatian provinces." Of course, the people of Vares did not see that as a good solution, and no one -- I say no one in Bosnia-Herzegovina was able to satisfy all the appetites. This was a compromise. Precisely so. A great many Croats would stay outside the Croatian canton, and the same goes for the Bosniaks and Serbs, but this is all conditionally speaking. And this is the way Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be set up, to be both a national or ethnic and a civil state. This is not Praljak's plan, but Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Continuing down, I'm going to move down about six lines, you say: "Now we have got what we want, the homogenisation of our population continues. We can only fence off what is ours and build there our own space, our own state. It is all as clear as noon on a spring day." Now, General, those are your words, aren't they? This is your vision for Vance-Owen, homogenisation of population, population movement, ultimately where the peoples are living separately in homogenous -- ethnically-homogenous zones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not my plan or my vision. This was my scientific forecast which came about in full, with our without Praljak sitting in The Hague. Just look at today's Bosnia-Herzegovina and you will see that in totality my scientific forecast came about, in terms of the postwar migrations, as we could also witness after the First World War, the Second World War, and so on and so forth. I think I was fully right at that time, as I am now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Unless there's more questions about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. Before you proceed further, I would also like to ask a question about these two last lines in English on that very page, 52, and both you and Mr. Praljak spoke about the homogenisation. My question is that -- to Mr. Praljak, by which methods did you think that homogenisation is going to continue, as you put it there? And my second question is relating to the very last line in the English text, to the very last line here, when it says -- and when you said that: "We can only fence off what is ours and build there our own space and our own state." And here I would like to ask you: What was your idea about your -- to put your words, I quote again, "our own state"? So what did you think about that, and how did you want to achieve this goal, that is, to "build our own space and our own state"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will first respond to your second question, Your Honour. I do not agree that this person interpreted my utterance well, the creation of our space and building our own state, because it was not supposed to be a state. As here, the pace of my speech was a problem for him as well, and I don't think it was correct. As far as I recall, I never discussed a state or the fencing off of a territory. This goes against what I had previously said. Secondly, to respond to your first question, I did not discuss homogenisation at all by certain means. I foresaw that this would come about as a natural consequence of the war and the growing problems. Much as the natural consequence of homogenisation would be -- or, rather, was in Hungary, Romania, et cetera, there is natural migration, and then after the war with Turkey there was a situation with Ataturk and Turkey, where half a million people were moved about, then half a million of Germans after the Second World War. These are simply scientific facts that I have no impact on, and this is what occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Look at the homogenisation process in Bosnia-Herzegovina nowadays. 210.000 Croats in Republika Srpska are not there, they are not coming back. Sarajevo has 95 or 96 per cent of Muslims, and this is so. These are natural laws coming about after wars. Every year, in terms of statistics, 10 per cent of any expelled population is not going to return. If you fail to return them by the end of five or six years, they will no longer return. These are world statistics that I'm familiar with, nothing more than that. I was just saying what the consequences of the war would be, independent of my will. As a lad said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, thank you very much for your answer. Mr. Stringer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Praljak, I don't want to put you in a difficult situation, but you're saying that the young man who made the minutes might have misinterpreted your words. That might have happened. Things happen. But when looking at the text, a number of questions spring to mind. Before all this, you say that there is no state without a nation, so you're already mentioning this question of state. You're mentioning the state on several occasions, which is why my fellow Judge put this question to you, and I was going to put exactly the same question to you. According to the Vance-Owen Plan, the only state is the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is no other state than that one, so why are you talking about a state? You seem to say that there's no state without a nation, but in the background you're talking about the Croatian nation, so those who do not have your standing, your education, your culture, might listen to you and interpret by saying, "Well, Slobodan Praljak is telling us that there's a need for a Croatian state."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Vance-Owen Plan, luckily it failed. Well, Croats started moving out en masse, Your Honours. They were given Croatian citizenship at the outset, and as this guy told me, he said, Mr. Praljak, for the third time my family is rebuilding its home in this century, and I will not do it the fourth time 'round. These are people who were expelled, who were at war, who were being killed. They didn't want to live there anymore. If they had relatives in France or Germany, they went. If they had someone in Croatia, they did go. We were fighting for the survival of the minimum number of Croats who were still there, which in the meantime the figures of which were halved. People flee unless they are protected, unless there is -- their national and citizen identities are protected. These are facts. Anyone dealing in sociology knows this. Croats happen to be a nation with the greatest number of emigres among nations. People in Vares said, Well, we'll no longer live there, so what can I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As my fellow Judge Trechsel told you earlier, you're not directly answering my questions or his questions. I had a very specific question. I was asking you whether during this meeting you uttered the word "state" on several occasions, and instead of answering my question, and everybody agrees with you, you're saying in this kind of situation some people migrate. Fine, we can only agree with you on that, on that statement of facts, but you're not answering my question. I wanted to know whether you uttered the word "state." You're saying, well, the young man who took the minutes made a mistake. He might have made one mistake, but making the same mistake over and over again, because the word "state" occurs in that text many times, you must have talked about state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, it was about Bosnia-Herzegovina. You saw hundreds of documents referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina, but unless the Croatian people are specifically protected, we would disappear. This specific protection was entailed within the Vance-Owen, Cutileiro, and Stoltenberg plan. They were based on the protection of the least numerous nation. Unfortunately, the last plan, the Dayton one, no longer protected it, and I don't think there are more than 450.000 left. This is about Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had to be set up to protect the basic principles: One, the right of a nation to exist; and the right of a citizen to enjoy his or her rights. And that was not done. The smallest nation, albeit they have their national state, were forced to leave the other one because they could not enjoy all of the rights and privileges because they were not protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, concerning your latest two questions, and this is something that was discussed even before that, we discussed the value of this note or these minutes. This is not a transcript. These are notes. For technical reasons, I wanted to have on the record that on the 5th of September, 2006, the same topic was discussed, when we saw this document for the first time with Witness Tomljanovich. The question is whether the words of the participants were conveyed truly and fully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours. And here it says "and we have it now." This means we have the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It comes right after "there is no state without a nation." It is clear. If there are no inhabitants, then all the rest is in vain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, since you challenged the text that's being attributed to you here in this meeting, I want to come back to this issue for one moment, these words: "Now we have got what we want, the homogenisation of our population continues, we can only fence off what is ours and build there our own state --" I'm sorry, "our own space and our own state. It is all as clear as noon on a spring day." Now, General, if you would look at the screen, I'm going to show you some transcript of your testimony in this trial on the 4th of June, 2009, page 41242. We've got it in Sanction. I'll read to you beginning from line 21. These are your words in the transcript: "At this point in time, we are in Stolac --" Let me interrupt here. You were talking about one of the presidential transcripts, where there was discussion with President Tudjman about how far you should fight or defend, and you said: "At this point in time, we are in Stolac and we stopped right there. It's about the president saying, don't move further from there, don't launch a defence war. We defended all the areas from Republika Srpska and from the JNA, the Muslim and Croat majority areas, and stopped right there." Continuing on to the next page, you say: "These are the facts of the matter, and that's as clear as a spring day." Now, General, it's interesting that the phrase you used two months ago in this trial, "clear as a spring day," is, in fact, the same phrase, virtually, that's attributed to you by the person who took these minutes, and I'm going to put to you, General, that, in fact, the person that wrote these minutes down wrote them accurately and that, in fact, he accurately reported your words that you said on that day in April 1993. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems your knowledge is immense if you know that a person could take down everything I said, even though we have professional interpreters here who constantly object to the pace of my speech. As for someone taking down my phrase, saying that something was as clear as the noon on a spring day, cannot mean that -- or does not mean that he correctly recorded the sentence preceding that. In any case, I stand by the fact that my political and scientific position is clear, and that is that this young man could not take down correctly everything I said and that hundreds of other documents expressing -- containing my views can amend or serve as an addition to everything I said, in terms of the official Croatian policy and the policy of the HZ-HB. This was said on numerous times. Yes, Bosnia-Herzegovina; yes, three constituent peoples. And the state was supposed to be set up to the benefit of all three and not to the detriment of any. Unfortunately, this did not materialise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Prosecutor did not put a question to you, but in the text we see that Mr. Kordic is it taking the floor to talk about Zenica. Take a look at it and look at what he says. After that, you will leave the meeting with Mr. Coric, but he's talking about creating a municipality in Zenica, and he's saying that instructions were given. In Zenica, there's a Muslim component. So how can you reconcile all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the census, in Zenica there were 30.000 Croats, Judge Antonetti, 30.000 Croats in Zenica, approximately. This was a rather compact area. For example, the Jura Sema [phoen] Canton in the Federation, I think in 1965, separated and became an independent unit without undermining the foundations of the Swiss state. Well, if something like that existed, then there was no reason not to implement such a good model of organisation of a state in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These incredible experiments were conducted there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have the census figures for Zenica. This is in document 10519. In 1991, in Zenica, there's 145.517 people; 22.000 Croats, 80.000 Muslims. So if elections are held, the 80.000 Muslims will lead the municipality. They're in the majority, and the Croats are in a minority. You can't deny that. So why is Mr. Kordic saying that there's a need to create a municipality? The figures don't allow for this. How can you interpret what Mr. Kordic is saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This homogenisation, Your Honours, that we discussed did take place in Bosnia-Herzegovina on a miniature scale. The number of Croats kept coming down. The Croats in Zenica lived in a relatively compact area. We can annex them to Jajce municipality or to Travnik and thus realise an absolute or maximum Croat majority, leaving the rest of the territory to Muslims, where they would have 98 per cent. You can draft borders in such a way all across Bosnia-Herzegovina and that you would always end up with a relative majority of Muslims. But the Vance-Owen simply foresaw elections. For example, in Jablanica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, if I'm wrong, please correct me. The Geneva meeting, all the work done, the Vance-Owen Plan, all this was done based on statistics that came from the census figures; you agree with me on this. So when they decided to create Cantons 3, 8, and 10, where there's a Croat majority, they base themselves on statistics. So unless I'm wrong, in the international community people integrated the fact that elections would be held in these cantons and those who were in a majority would remain in the majority. Do you agree on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree. This is Kordic's idea of sorts. I cannot interpret him. I agree with you in full, that this was the basic plan of setting up Bosnia and Herzegovina from Cutileiro onwards. That was the guiding thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I don't know is it proper or not, but this is already in evidence. We introduced evidence as Vance-Owen Plan and all documents. It is not true that this democratic strict principle is going to be applied. For every province is envisaged how many in government. For instance, 10 of them should be Croat, Serb, or Muslim. So those right are going to be protected. I just want to add something which was already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will refer to that. It may be time for the break. It's 10.30. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, before we continue with the next document, I want to take a short -- hopefully what will be a short detour and take you back to a little piece of your testimony from yesterday. This is when we were discussing the videotape that showed the oath-taking ceremony for the Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica in December of 1992. Do you recall when we looked at that video yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in response, I believe, to a question from His Honour Judge Antonetti, you were asked about whether there was a flag for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna - this is page 72 of yesterday's transcript - and you said: "Well, I don't think that any decree proclaimed it as such, that the Republic of Herceg-Bosna -- Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna proclaiming that. It didn't have a hymn or a flag. It was a flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, quite simply, nothing more than that." So you were describing the flags that were being shown during that ceremony, and I wanted to clarify this, General. Are you saying that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have a flag, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, really. First of all, it's not the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. That came later with a proposed agreement on the part of the international community. As far as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna goes, I don't know whether there are any documents proscribing any form of state flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'd like for us to take a look at P00772. Mr. President, it's just something -- it's already admitted into evidence. It's a decree from the Narodni List, and I'm simply proposing that since it's already in evidence we can show it in e-court on the screen just to make this brief point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, do you see the document on the screen in front of you? Do you see this is the decree on the coat of arms for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is from 1992, prior to the time of this -- about a month prior to the time of this celebration or this ceremony in Zenica. So I'm not suggesting that you did know, General, either way whether or not there was a flag, but would you agree with me it appears that, in fact, there had been a decree on a -- what we could call a coat of arms and flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that a decree existed on the use of a coat of arms and a flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. However, at the same time it's always important to mention that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was within the frameworks of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it says here, and that it was established as a temporary solution for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. General, we can move back to the binder for what I think is going to be the last exhibit in this set, and I'd like to take you to Exhibit P02719 which is one of the presidential transcripts from the 11th of June, 1993. 2719. It should be behind the document that we were just looking at, although I may have skipped one. P02719. General, if you don't have it, tell us, and we can -- we can --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't find it. I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, we do not have it either, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I referred to the same transcript earlier. It's in, I think, the next previous binder, and so we probably didn't include it again. But if it's not handy, I'm actually inclined to skip over it at this point, rather than taking a lot of time. Could I propose, since this is from one of the presidential transcripts, perhaps we could try to work off e-court, and if the general is able to do that and if that works okay with everyone, it's just one reference to this transcript I'd like to go to and then we can move on. So this is P02719, if we could get that up in e-court. It's a record of a presidential -- meeting at the Presidency. I'll start over again. It's the minutes -- it's the record of the meeting between President Tudjman and others, together with President Izetbegovic and his contingent, in Zagreb on the 11th of June, 1993, and I want to go to page 17 of this transcript. Just actually for reference, so that we can remember, if we look at page 16, we'll see -- and this is the part we looked at earlier in your cross-examination, General, where President Izetbegovic was questioning President Tudjman about the role or the activities of people like Mr. Boban, Mr. Kordic, Mr. Kostroman, and Tudjman says here on page 16 that the only message that they were receiving from "us," that is, the Croatian side, in Zagreb was to cooperate. So that's the part that we looked at earlier. And now turning the page, I want to go with some of the statements of President Izetbegovic on page 17. He's talking about events and tensions between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he says, and I'm going to go to about the middle of the page: "How it all came about and how it came in such a response, the bitter cup overflowed, overflowed with that behaviour with Mostar, Ahmici, Prozor, convoys with food, convoys with weapons, that was all stopped, plundered day after day; they have been enduring all this for a year, in the middle of their own country they have to come, an HVO pass is signed for 50 marks, all this is endured until it comes to this, and then this happens. I condemn these things, but I am simply trying to explain how such excesses occur. Believe me that the violence perpetrated down there by the HVO, the arbitrary acts perpetrated down there by the HVO - and they were better armed than our people - exceeds all bounds ..." And then Izetbegovic asks Tudjman: "Did you recognise a parallel army? We said, okay, we have to recognise it, and then we continued to fight the Chetniks, et cetera, and we said that it was a lawful army and that cost us. Now it goes a step further. Boban, instead of accepting, recognising the army, now wants a state as well; he doesn't want any Bosnian signs there; he wants to cleanse the population. The Muslims move. Then invents that there are 100 or 200.000 more because of the refugees, that this upsets the demographic structure. They have to be cleansed, et cetera. This other argument of yours, perhaps it explains some things. It says there were Muslims, their percentage was such and such, now it has changed because of the refugees. So what should be done? They should be cleansed, driven away. You know what happened in Mostar. They came up to people who were not refugees, to people who lived there from way back. The Ustashas did not do that, Mr. Tudjman. Mostar was under the Ustashas for four years. There was Bajedic's [phoen] house, that very same Bajedic who was with the partisans up there. The family remained behind, and nobody drove them away in those four years, while Boban's men drove out thousands of families from their homes in Mostar, occupied the houses, and ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we are now in June of 1993, General. We're two months after this meeting that we were just talking about that you participated in in Central Bosnia. We're two months after Izetbegovic's signing the Vance-Owen Plan, and yet still he's continuing -- or he's complaining about expulsions not only of refugees, Muslim refugees, but now long-time Muslim residents of places like Mostar, and I've got two questions here. First of all, the fact is now that we know that on the ground, these so-called protections of the Muslims or the minorities that you've been talking about that were going to take place under Vance-Owen, in fact, never came to pass and that the only thing that happened post-April 1993 was the continued expulsion of Muslims from the so-called Croatian territory; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is wholly untrue, everything that Izetbegovic says and everything that you're saying, quite untrue. In April in Mostar, it wasn't the HVO making any plans to attack the BH Army. It was Pasalic who made plans to attack -- just a moment, I beg your pardon. My answer is that Izetbegovic -- yes. Well, I said it's incorrect. All that is not true. It's just a lot of rattling, blah-blah-blah, that's all it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you deny that large numbers of Muslim inhabitants of Mostar were being evicted and driven away by the HVO during June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know what it is that Mr. Izetbegovic is speaking about here. I know that on the 9th of May, the BH Army attacked Mostar and the HVO, and it was -- the situation was precisely the reverse. It was on the side controlled by the BH Army that only 140 Croats were left, whereas on the other side more than 7.000 Muslims remained, and those are the facts. So Izetbegovic is not telling the truth. He is doing a bit of political manipulation here. And, secondly, when he speaks about the Ustashas, he forgets to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. I'll put it to you again. Do you deny that large numbers of Muslim inhabitants of Mostar were being evicted and driven away by the HVO during June of 1993? Do you deny that or do you accept that that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell us how many. What large numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you're playing games with me, and we're not going to play games. You've sat in this courtroom for the past three years. You've heard the evidence. You've heard the witnesses come talk about what happened to them in Mostar. You've heard others who were there, who were acting as internationals. I'm asking you, and I'm talking about hundreds of Muslims from Mostar being driven out of flats, out of apartments, in June, driven across to the eastern side of Mostar. Do you accept that that was taking place or do you deny it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I heard here, and only according to that, I could agree that 200 to 300 Muslims from the western side, which was controlled by the HVO, was, by groups outside anybody's control, expelled to the eastern side. Whether it was 200 or 150, I don't know. But I also know that the organised HVO protected more than 7.000 Muslims who throughout the war remained on the west side. So that's why I'm asking you what numbers you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. When Izetbegovic here, in this conversation, regrets recognising an army, a parallel army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Stringer. I believe Mr. Petkovic wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Could the microphone be adjusted. Thank you. The microphone does not seem to be working. The microphone is still not working. We can't hear General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now? Yes, thank you. A technical question would be in order related to the 11th of June, 1993, the day when Mr. Izetbegovic was in Zagreb. That would be interesting. I think that General Praljak has forgotten this, so you can refresh his memory and he can confirm or deny it. Did Travnik definitely fall into the hands of the BH Army on that day, whereas Mr. Izetbegovic said not a word about that to Mr. Tudjman? That's all I have to say, because we have to tie in the context of that meeting and those talks with everything else. I don't know if Praljak is aware of this or knows about it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know that, and I'm claiming that Izetbegovic is just telling political lies here and is referring to Boban and the Croats. First of all, his interlocutor was not Franjo Tudjman but a legally -- the legally elected representatives of the Croatian people. The fact that the convoy did not pass through, well, who did he fight against? You saw hundreds of documents to the effect that we provided weapons, and we took care of all the refugees and transported all the wounded people. These are blatant lies by a man leaving the Vance-Owen Plan and preparing an all-out attack by the BH Army, because the BH Army at this particular time expelled all the Croats from Travnik. What are we talking about here? Those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Praljak, what Mr. Petkovic said drew my attention to this meeting which took place between President Tudjman and Izetbegovic on the 11th of June, 1993. I realised that this took place at something like 1.00 in the morning, so a meeting that takes place at 1.00 in the morning is a serious meeting. There must be a valid reason for that. What happened on the 10th or the 11th of June which led to the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic had to meet Mr. Tudjman past midnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I know that on the 11th, the BH Army launched a mass attack expelling the HVO and the people from Travnik. I know that on the 9th of May, after preparations in April, that it attacked Mostar, that is to say, the HVO in Mostar. And I also know, and I said this several times, that they were preparing to take over Croatian territory or territory from the Croatians because they did not wish or could not fight the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, if we admit that on the 11th of June the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina drive out the Croats in Travnik, how is it, then, that on the same day Mr. Izetbegovic meets Mr. Tudjman? Is it to talk about this, to discuss it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Obviously, he wasn't telling him anything. Everything that Izetbegovic is saying here is a lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're looking at the transcript of this conversation, like I do, because Mr. Izetbegovic is complaining about the behaviour of the HVO and the attacks. If there had been the Travnik attack, Mr. Tudjman should have told him then, Well, what are you complaining about, since you have just attacked us, attacked me, attacked the HVO in Travnik? But this does not figure here. Does this mean that he didn't know about it, because he doesn't mention it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for getting up, but I'd just like to draw your attention to the fact that we don't have the transcript in front of us, at least most of us don't. But if we look at the second page of the transcript, then we'll see that President Tudjman is speaking about the fact that the BH Army attacked certain Croatian villages, and then about the events taking place on the territory inhabited by Croatians. So on the basis of just one page of the transcript, we're not going to be able to establish everything they discussed on that particular day, unless we look at the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partiality in this way won't lead us anywhere. Well, it will lead us somewhere, but not in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: For the record, first, if we look at the beginning of this meeting, we see that Mr. Izetbegovic is complaining because on TV he says he has seen HVO soldiers, Croatian fighters, received by the Serbs, and singing the praise of how well they were received. So one must assume that Alija Izetbegovic was fearing some kind of treason. Whether rightly or wrongly, I will not speculate at all. And, second, if there was an attack on Travnik on the 11th of June, it is not very reasonable, I think, to expect that Izetbegovic or Tudjman were informed of this at 25 past midnight, because that's the first minutes, and I cannot imagine, for the life of me, how at that moment they can already be informed of an attack which it is said took place on that day. So I think we better not speculate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, Serb Television or, rather, television of the Republika Srpska, was all too happy to broadcast that particular evening how refugees from Vlasic were escaping to Serb territory. That was televised, so people knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to ask us -- I'd just like to ask you to provide General Praljak with the entire text so that he can follow, because just extracting a single page or passage, without showing the whole text, I don't think will lead us to the right conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Actually, the observations I made are not opening a new discussion, but, on the contrary, showing that first there is an answer to the question the President has raised, there is an explanation why they met at that time, and, second, the logical difficulties in assuming that they might have known about the attack on Travnik. That's all, and I do not think that one has to have a document to take cognizance of this, and I think we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, I did not get up following on from your intervention, that was far from my mind. I was up on my feet before you started speaking and then I sat down, and I just wanted to ask the Prosecutor, very kindly, to provide General Praljak with the integral text if -- of the transcripts if he's going to discuss them. Just that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I should, then, apologise for having interrupted you or taken precedence. Please, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
