utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would propose, actually, to move on. I have got a hard copy of it here. The transcript was in the previous binder, but I think that I've exhausted my questions on this issue, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Mr. Stringer, but in which previous binder? We have been given three binders, so which one? It's not in any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The one just before this, the first of the JCE binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the summer recess; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one we were given before the recess; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Correct. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may assist, it's a binder labelled "List 3."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wonder whether we really need to stay with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on. General Praljak, I would like to have a clarification on Mr. Izetbegovic's personality. Sometimes you've said good things about him, sometimes bad things, and just now you did not say good things about him. Thanks to my colleague, we have been able to determine that on the 11th of June, there could be no question about the Travnik attack because a meeting was held after midnight. So had there been an attack, the attack would have taken place on the morning of the 11th of June. And in the transcript, we can see that Mr. Izetbegovic is complaining about the behaviour of the HVO. I see here -- there's no need to look at the text. You can trust me. On page 12 of the English, Mr. Izetbegovic says: "Last night I ordered a cease-fire, a unilateral cease-fire." So he says to Mr. Tudjman, I have ordered a cease-fire. And a few hours after that, they attack. How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Izetbegovic did not have control of his army, or Halilovic in particular, on many counts, or the commanders in Zenica. So whether intentionally or not -- well, whether he's telling the truth or lying, I can't go into that, but the facts refute what he says completely. So as -- nobody listened to his orders on the cease-fire, none of the BH Army, if he actually did issue those orders, or perhaps he just said he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just be allowed to say one more sentence? Is it possible that -- it is possible that you didn't understand what General Petkovic said. General Petkovic did not say that on that day, that is to say, the 11th of June, is when the attack on Travnik began, but that Travnik fell, that is to say, that the BH attack had been completed in such a way as Travnik fell. The attack went on for several days, so both President Izetbegovic and President Tudjman knew of the attack. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the answer to Judge Antonetti would be this: On page 2 of the transcript, for heaven's sake, Mr. Izetbegovic says that he watched television that evening, and President Tudjman says he didn't see anything -- he wasn't watching television, and he says the armies of the Serb Republic are receiving the Croatian fighters who are boasting. Of course, they have to boast to prevent them from being killed. They say how they were taken in. And he says, We could have foreseen this a long time ago, because this cooperation has existed for a long time. This is morbid. It's a false, morbid lie. I can accept that Mr. Izetbegovic really doesn't know what was going on there, that they attacked Travnik, massacred the people, and that he says that was because of cooperation with the Serbs. That's just idiocy. So that's his level of information. Now, what he knows, what he doesn't know of the situation, I don't know, but it's all morbid, very morbid. And then he says that we didn't provide any food. Well, for heaven's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you can put away that binder. Actually, you can put away both of the binders that are in front of you, because we're going to move to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can help you and bring you the next binder which I believe she has. This would be a binder that says "List 5," binder 1 of 2. These were distributed to everyone yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, we're shifting gears. We're going to talk for a while about the HVO military and how it was structured and how it operated, and we're going to talk a bit about your position as commander of the HVO. And I want to start off with the testimony that you gave a few years ago, when you were a defence witness in the Naletilic-Martinovic case, Tuta Stela. This is from -- your testimony is Exhibit P10980, and on page 9419 of that transcript, and I know you don't have it in the Croatian language because we don't have that, so we're going to put it on the screen and we can -- I can read you the parts, and you can take the interpretation. You were asked -- actually, while we're there, General, why don't you turn to the next document in your binder, which is the chart that you were writing on when you testified in the Tuta Stela case. There you go, you've got it. There's an organisation chart that should have your handwriting on it, if you turn one more page. That's right. Okay. And so for the record, the General's testimony from the Tuta Stela trial is, for our case here, marked as P10980, and then the organisational chart that the general worked with when he was testifying as a witness in the Tuta Stela case, our exhibit number for that is P09324, just so that we don't confuse those numbers with the exhibit numbers from the Tuta Stela case. So, General, let me ask you -- I'm going to read some of your testimony to you, and we will refer also to the chart that you had in front of you at the time you testified back in April of 2002, and this was on your direct examination. And at that time, Mr. Krsnik, who was the lawyer for Mladen Naletilic, was asking you some questions about the HVO organisation, and he says - this is page 9419 of the Tuta Stela transcript at line 7: "And I will start now by asking you about the structure of the HVO at the time when you arrived, as of the 28th of July -- 27th of July, 1993, onward." And let me stop there, General. Now, these have indications that you took command of the HVO on the 27th of July, 1993, but I believe we've established, actually, that it was the 24th of July which is the day you took command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And you were first asked about Mladen Naletilic, and you were asked if you knew him personally, and you said, yes, you knew him personally. You had known each other since childhood. And so as you've already testified, you knew each other when you were school-aged children, and then you met again many years later after he returned from abroad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From your question, one could conclude that we attended school together. We attended school in the same building, but he is younger than I am. We were not in the same class. I think there were two years of difference between the two of us. At that time, it was quite a difference, because I always tried to hang out with those older than me. In any case, I did know him. Everyone knew everyone else in that small place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then turning the page of the transcript, Mr. Krsnik is asking you about this chart here which we're looking at, which in the Tuta Stela trial was marked as Exhibit D1/82, and he says to you or he asks -- asks you to look at the chart. And you say: "This is more or less an accurate chart of the HVO structure in 1993." And he asks you to be more specific, and then this is what you say: "First comes the supreme commander, then the Defence Department. Then below it is the Main Staff. The military police units are attached to the Defence Department. The Main Staff has command over four operative zones, Operative Zone Mostar, Tomislavgrad, Vitez, Orasje. And directly tied to the Main Staff are units attached to the Main Staff, and special purpose units and professional units are directly related to the Main Staff through the Defence Department and then on, that is upward, to the supreme commander." And then you're asked about special-purpose units or the so-called ATGs, which in English stands for "anti-terrorist group," and you say: "Yes, I'm familiar with the term 'ATG.' These are mostly units that would go to the front-line at a particular point in time, perform a task, and then go back home, in point of fact, because there were no barracks. And in those instances when they stayed on the front-line, then they would be subordinated to the commander of that particular front-line." Okay. General, just first question on what I read to you so far is: What you said under oath in the Naletilic-Martinovic case back in April of 2002, do you still consider that to be a correct general description of the HVO structure for our purposes today? And we're going to talk about this in more detail, obviously, and so I'm just trying to get a general response from you as to this sort of overview that you've provided to Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I said that it was more or less correct. It is because on the 24th, I was appointed commander of the Main Staff, not of the HVO, as you put it, and I was immediately in the midst of the war and the effort to defend ourselves against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was familiar with what was going on in the field. I didn't participate in the making of -- drawing up of any structure or hierarchy of the HVO, in military -- in the military sense. Therefore, I'm not the right person to ask general questions of. I can tell you only whether at that moment I could command a unit or not, and I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire structure was created earlier. I was put in the midst of the war, and while I was there it was fierce. The only thing I asked for was for the Main Staff, the four men -- well, allow me to tell you the basic thing. Later on, you'll move on to areas to which I won't be able to give you answers to and some things that I won't be able to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me try to break it down to come back to what you told the Judges back in April of 2002 in the Tuta Stela case, and we can walk down the chart. First of all, do you remember that the writing here is writing that you made, that you were asked to make on the chart when you were testifying in that case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made the notes, according to my best knowledge and recollection. But when I said "more or less accurate," that is important. I'm not certain of any schematics. I simply didn't participate in the drawing up of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So that from your Tuta Stela testimony, when you said that this is more or less accurate, then you continue to hold that view today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less accurate, yes. I don't know whether it's accurate, though. I know some things for sure, such as operational zones, et cetera, but as I've said several times about certain professional units, well, I can answer to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Well, then, just to break it down a little bit, here at the top of the chart we have a box for the position of supreme commander, and can we agree that actually at all times during 19 -- during 1993, that Mate Boban was the supreme commander of the HVO military?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I commanded the Main Staff, Mr. Boban was the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then on the chart, moving down, then we have the Defence Department, and here you indicated, back when you testified before, that Bruno Stojic was the head of the Defence Department, and can we agree that that was the case during the time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I commanded the Main Staff of the HVO, Mr. Bruno Stojic was head of the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just a couple of questions about the time prior to when you took command of the Main Staff. You were present in Prozor in October of 1992, shortly after the conflict took place there; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We know that you spent a lot of time in that Prozor-Tomislavgrad region throughout the earlier part of 1993, before you took command of the Main Staff; isn't that also true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't agree about this being a lot of time. I was specific as to when, where, with what purpose, and what I said. You are referring to Tomislavgrad, but I didn't go there often. There is precise information about when, where, in what time, and with what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were in Mostar, I believe, on the 11th or the 10th of May, correct, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were involved in combat activities in the Boksavica area in June and early July of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were in the Gornji Vakuf area in mid-January of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 15th of January and the 23rd of January, in the morning, in Rama, and only a bit in Uskoplje to see what the situation was and to share with the commanders there what my view of the situation was, as well as to carry out the task, or, rather, I consented to going there with a certain purpose in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We know, from the document we looked at earlier today, that you were present in Central Bosnia in the early part of April of 1993, when you were participating in the meeting with Colonel Blaskic, Dario Kordic, and the others. So we agree you were in Central Bosnia in -- on the 2nd of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So all of this is to simply suggest to you that even before you took command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, you had a great deal of contact and involvement in the HVO so that you are able to tell us that, in fact, Bruno Stojic was the head of the Defence Department during this entire period of time that we've been talking about, beginning from October of 1992 onward, correct, until --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. Contacts and actual knowledge are two different things. I was in contact with Mr. Stojic, but as to what he became at what time and when he was appointed to what position, I don't know. You have documents based on which you can conclude that. I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then on this chart, underneath the Defence Department we've got the Main Staff, the "Glavni Stozer" which you took command of in -- on the 24th of July, 1993. Now, can we agree, General, that the Main Staff within the structure was a part of the Defence Department? I don't want to talk about who had authority to order or the differing responsibilities and roles that were played, but in terms of the organisational structure, can't we agree that the Main Staff fell within the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can, and yet we cannot. That is not completely true. The command structure of the Main Staff started with Mate Boban and with me, but parts of that structure also rely on the Defence Department, which entails a number of functions in relation to the army. This was widely discussed. This is linked to Mate Boban and Main Staff and the Defence Department and then, in turn, to the government. One cannot simplify matters and twist them so that they become untrue. We can only discuss them to the point at which the true nature of mutual relations are -- become distorted. Once we're there, that is no longer true and it is no longer a simplification but cheating.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Defence Department's responsibilities in respect of the Main Staff included such things as logistics and mobilisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but not only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then when we talk about the Defence Department --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mobilisation? I don't know exactly who was in charge of that. I don't want to tell you anything I'm not sure of. I cannot answer precisely who was in charge of mobilisation, its implementation, et cetera. I'm not sure. Therefore, the Main Staff was not in charge of mobilisation. That is what I can tell you for certain. As to who was in charge, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask it this way, then, since you were in charge of the Main Staff from the 24th of July: Did the Main Staff look to the Defence Department to -- as the responsible organ for logistics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We received that from the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, we turned to the Logistics Department. When units required supplies, they always asked that from the Main Supplies Base, and I guess the base, in turn, received its supplies within -- Mr. Stringer, I can precisely answer your technical questions, but in terms of organisations of this type, I'm not the best interlocutor for that, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you telling us, General, that at the time you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, you don't actually know what entity was responsible for logistics for your army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. The Main Logistics Base of the HVO was the organ in charge. The various units turned to it when they needed supplies. The operational zones asked for supplies, in terms of staffing and weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it the Defence Department that ran the Logistics Base, that was responsible for ensuring that the required logistics were taking place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct answer would be that the Logistics Base was not run by the Main Staff. It is highly likely, according to the information I have, that it was run by the Defence Department. It is correct that it was not run by the Main Staff, and most likely it fell within the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, there's no other place for it to fall, isn't there? If it's not the Defence Department, then it's -- there's no other body that's going to be responsible for that. General, I'm going to suggest to you that you're not being candid with me on basic issues such as this. Don't we both know that logistics and Logistics Centre fell within the jurisdiction of the HVO Defence Department and Bruno Stojic, at least from the 24th of July, 1993, to the 9th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm being completely candid. I simply want to be mathematically precise. The man in charge was for sure not appointed by the Main Staff. I say that it is highly likely -- well, if you tell me to put my life on that, that it was the Defence Department, well, I'd rather not. I didn't have time to study this in detail, and you better ask someone else to get a precise answer. I know, with mathematical -- if I knew with mathematical certainty, I wouldn't try avoiding any question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we agree that as we move down the chart, that the four operative zones that you testified about, that you identified in the Naletilic-Martinovic trial, that the operative zones, and the brigades, and the units falling under those operative zones, were directly subordinated to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, let's move off to the side, then, and talk about a more complicated issue which relates to the professional units -- special units, professional units, and perhaps these anti-terrorist groups. Now, as I understand from your testimony in the Naletilic-Martinovic case, and this is at page 9576 of that transcript, you've said, and I'm looking at line 12 -- you're being asked about these ATGs or professional units, and you've said that you had two such units, that was the Bruno Busic and the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, as being two professional units that were directly subordinated to the Main Staff. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not brigades, but regiments. Therefore, that were less men. That is correct. With Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic, those were the two units that I could command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as I understand from your earlier testimony, these two units were professional, in that the members of these two units stayed attached to the unit all the time, they didn't go home, for example, and over time they were staying -- or that they stayed in barracks together, as opposed to going home. Is that something that distinguished them from other units of the HVO that were not professional units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. One of the things that distinguished them was that when they weren't up in at their positions in an action of some kind, they were -- well, the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion in Capljina, Mr. Stringer, they were dispersed. They weren't in one part. They had their parts in Central Bosnia and so on. So when I say this, it turns out that the entire regiment, as many as they were, that they were all in one place, which is not true. They weren't, while I was down there, of course, as opposed to the others who, when they did their seven-day shifts or twelve-day shifts, would go home and become civilians. The members of these two units, on the other hand, were always at the disposal of who needed them. You didn't have to mobilise them all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if you needed them and if you needed to deploy members of these two units into combat operations, you had the authority to do so directly? You didn't have to consult, for example, with another body, such as the Defence Department, in order to coordinate such a deployment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I did that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that is different from other units that did require some coordination or approval from the Defence Department before they could be deployed; is that true? For example, a military police unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, I received approval, at my request, so that the military police units, because of the situation, in the military sense could be subordinated, and those units of the military police which were -- well, the battalions, military police battalions, the professional ones, I could send them out into an action without having to consult anybody further because I was given a general approval, an overall approval, from Mate Boban through Bruno Stojic, or the two of them together, whatever. And once I received this overall approval, the military police battalions, made up of professionals, well, I could deploy them, I could send them to the battle-front, without having to seek additional authority from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that the situation that was in existence throughout the entire time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, that you or the Main Staff could deploy military police battalions as though they were one of the other units that was directly subordinated to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I can't really answer your question because it's been a long time since then. Perhaps it's true that sometime in October 1993, perhaps, that decision was declared null and void, and when the 1993 Muslim offensive was completely routed and when there was not only a cessation of hostility but when the situation became calmer, I can't actually remember whether at that particular point in time that right was rescinded, the right to deploy the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Maybe it's more accurate to say that this special arrangement, where the Main Staff could directly deploy military police units, is linked to the situation with the Operation Neretva and the needs that arose in connection with that ABiH operation, so that as the needs diminished over time, then it may be that this special arrangement was no longer needed and, therefore, no longer in force?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is highly possible. I am not sure of that. But let's not refer to it as a special arrangement. It was a logical military development. Once you have defence as the basis of every such system and when there was the danger that we, from Central Bosnia to the south of Mostar, could be routed, and that the BH Army, which wished to emerge along the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was afoot, then it is logical to use all your elements of defence, including the military police, in your defence against the attacker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to intervene. I wonder if I could ask the Registrar's assistance in getting somebody from the computer help desk. My LiveNote has frozen, and I've tried restarting it. So if we could get some assistance, I would be most grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, to your understanding, then, this -- the arrangement -- the approval, I should say, the approval that you obtained from Mate Boban to directly deploy military police units was not an arrangement that was in effect prior to the time you became commander of the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably that is correct, but I don't know whether it is wholly correct. I know what I told you, that that is what I requested and that is what I was given. What happened before was probably different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The -- in all likelihood, the arrangement or the system in place prior to Operation Neretva was one whereby if the Main Staff wanted to deploy or to have military police units at its disposal, it would seek the approval of the head of the Defence Department in order to deploy military police; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do object. In my respectful submission, this has been asked and answered. General Praljak said at -- in the last question, his answer is the answer he's already given, and he's not sure about what happened previously. Your Honour, it seems to be that my learned friend is seeking the witness to speculate beyond the area that he is willing or able to speak about, so I don't know if this is of assistance to the Court and to Your Honours in going further on an area where the witness has already spoken at least twice about the scope of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, prior to 24 July 1993, were you aware of any similar authorisation by made Boban or anyone else that permitted the Main Staff to directly deploy military police units without at least coordinating it with the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that authorisation was given to Tihomir Blaskic, not the Main Staff but the head of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, because he was in that kind of military situation whereby most probably seeking authorisation all the time wouldn't have been actually viable. But as I say, I requested authorisation and was given authorisation to -- for military deployment, that is to say, up at the lines for certain military police battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And since we're talking -- excuse me. Since we're talking about Operation Neretva, then, we're talking about deploying military police units into the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, they were deployed. Not all of them, and not all at the same time, of course, because they had to have shifts and so on, but a part of the military police was attached to the operative zone which was commanded by Miljenko Lasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And since you sought the authorisation of Mate Boban in order to do that, can we then agree that this was -- this was a change, this was something that required a special arrangement or an authorisation for Boban, because under normal circumstances the Main Staff could not deploy military police into that operative zone without the approval of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could agree with that as being a logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would you agree with the same premise if it was applied to the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone commanded by Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same rule would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me again. And as you've said, because of the different circumstances in Central Bosnia, a different authorisation had been given to Tihomir Blaskic whereby he could directly use military police units in that Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, so to the best of my recollections, I think that he had such authorisation, in view of the fact that, in communication terms, he was in a very difficult position, so he wasn't able to -- well, the military situation would sometimes dictate that a certain number of military policemen should, of course, take part in the defence of the area and territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're going to talk about the military police more at a later time, but one final question on this -- on this topic, because on the chart we can see -- we've been talking about this box off to the right which relates to the professional units or the ATGs. Off to the left, we have the military police units. And at any time, can we agree, General, that whenever a unit was deployed into an operative zone, whether it was a military police unit or whether it was a professional unit or an ATG, that no matter where they came from, they were going to be directly subordinated to the command of the operative zone? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several ATG groups, and I didn't command them. However, when they were in the operative zone and when they were given their assignment, in the operations sense, they were subordinated to the operative zone commander, or sector, or whatever, whatever geographic division according to the military situation in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the same holds true for a military police unit that is deployed into an operative zone; isn't that also true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. If the military police were deployed, then they would come under, in the operational sense - let me repeat that, in the operational sense - under the command of the commander of that particular operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again we'll talk about this in greater detail later, but when you're -- you're emphasizing the operational sense, and what that means is that these units remain linked to or they remain within the structure of the organisation that they came from? For example, a military police battalion remains within the military police structure even if it's been deployed to a position in an operative zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document in your binder is another one of these charts, and this is one of the ones that was shown to you during an earlier part of your testimony. I think it was during cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question before we move on to the next document. I'm still on the document which you authenticated when you signed it and testified in the Naletilic case. This is Exhibit P904 in the Naletilic case. As I understand the organisational chart, the professional units are attached to the Defence Department, because there's a line there. You say, when you answered Mr. Stringer's question, that when these units are on the ground, they report to the operational zone. So I heard what you said, and I compare this with the situation in Mostar in the month of May. When Mr. Naletilic's units, perhaps military policemen even, arrest Muslim people, are they then placed under the operational control of the person commanding the operational zone in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they wouldn't be placed under anybody's control. What I'm saying holds true under the assumption that they agreed to be under somebody's control, like the Ludvig Pavlovic professional unit and the other one. What, what do you say? Baja Kraljevic, yes, and Bruno Busic and so on, those. As far as I know, and I do know, Mr. Naletilic, while I was in command, was not under my command, so he wasn't under anybody's control, the control of any commander who was under my control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, to be crystal clear, because this is an essential issue - I'm sure you've understood this - in the organisation chart we have before us, according to you there is a difference to be established between the professional units, i.e., those under the control, and you quote Pavlovic, for instance, from those that are not placed under any control, that of Naletilic, for instance, i.e., the Convicts Battalion. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I'm afraid that there might be some misunderstanding. Perhaps it's due to the English interpretation, but on page 68, line 9, it says that your question was "when the units of Mladen Naletilic, perhaps even the military policemen," and as it was recorded in the transcript, it appears that you placed the military police into Mladen Naletilic's units. So when Mr. Praljak answered the question, it was no longer clear whether he said that in Mostar you could not command the units of Mladen Naletilic or you could not command the military police units, so I think there was a whole confusion there probably due to the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we need to clarify this. In the Mostar operation, during which people are arrested, we have evidence that establish that some military policemen played a part in this sometimes. You told us that you weren't there, so you can't have been aware of what may have happened. But as far as you know, if military policemen arrested people, could they be placed under the operational control of the operational zone in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge at that time, no, and I'm saying from the time that I arrived the military police units, the battalions, were placed -- well, the possibility was there for them to be deployed, and they were deployed, and they were under the commands of the operative zone on the territory they were on. Now, while I was down there, I was not able to command, nor did I command, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and everything that he considered to be his unit, although this is a very dubious concept, what his unit was, and I don't know who could command him. I did not, and I don't know who did or who could have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Stringer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next Exhibit is 4D01280, and, General, you can -- should be able to find it in your binder there. It's a chart from the Petkovic Defence that I believe was shown to you during their cross-examination of you, and -- well, let me just read you your testimony about this. I've just got a limited number of questions. And I'm looking at page 42417 of the transcript, General, your testimony on the 2nd of July of 2009, and Ms. Alaburic is asking you about this document. And she says: "So look at this diagram. It was made strictly in keeping with the Decree on the Armed Forces. Take a look at the structure of the Defence Department. Does this structure correspond to what your knowledge is of the organisational structure of the Defence Department?" And you say: "Yes, I'm familiar with this document. This is the composition of it, this is that diagram." I just wanted to clarify that, General, your testimony on that is that this is an accurate depiction of the structure of the HVO, or this part -- these parts of the HVO, I should say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: I have no reason, sir, to doubt Ms. Alaburic, especially not General Petkovic, because he is far better acquainted with all of these things than I am. So it is -- what I know is quite certain, that there was an assistant or that there should have been an assistant for security, and then under him the SIS administration and the Military Police Administration below that. And I certainly know that there was a Sector for Morale Guidance and that there was a Health Sector, too. Now, of course, this Administration for Procurement, Technical, whatever, I've heard of all of this, but with a great deal of certainty, although not absolute certainty, I know about -- these three main sectors did exist within the Defence Department. Now, for every one of these ones, I don't know. As to the -- I know that repairs had to be made. Somebody had to find the money to do that, that there was a general public competition for the construction work that needed to be done, so these construction sectors, yes, probably they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, actually, in your testimony you used the word -- actually, it was put to you by Ms. Alaburic. She used the word "parallel" services, that within the Defence Department these were all parallel services within the Defence Department, which included the Main Staff, the Security Sector and these others. Would you agree that that's an accurate way to characterise this chart, all of these as parallel components within the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Which parallel structures are you referring to? What does "parallel" mean? I didn't understand what "parallel structures" actually means. There were structures. I don't know what parallel structures there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, that within the Defence Department, there are different components, and we see all these components, and each component has its own role and responsibilities, and that they're operating under the umbrella of the Defence Department in a parallel way, that is, each taking care of its own job. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You, in the Main Staff, you had your job. The people over in the Security Sector, they had their job. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not actually correct. It's like this: The Main Staff, of course, has quite a lot of links to the Defence Department, but it's not on a par with the Sector for Moral Guidance, for example, or Morale. According to the line of command, I'm responsible to Mate Boban, so it's a little more complex as far as the Main Staff is concerned. Bruno Stojic cannot appoint me or replace me, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have a question to put to Mr. Stringer. The organisational chart we have before us is an organisational chart which the OTP has prepared, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this chart is not prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor. It's prepared, I believe, by the Petkovic Defence. It's Exhibit 4D01280, and it was used by Ms. Alaburic in her cross-examination of the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for providing us with this precious piece of information. If I compare this organisation chart with the one we have seen earlier, which you authenticated in the Naletilic case, the position of the Main Staff is very different. The Main Staff, according to the first organisation chart, is placed under the Ministry of Defence, whereas in the second organisation chart it's on the same level as Civilian Protection, Logistics, Healthcare. Do you agree with the organisation chart of the Petkovic Defence or don't you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, before General Praljak answers this question. I wanted to say that these two organograms are incomparable. They show completely different things. The organogram that was drafted in the Naletilic case in a way speaks of the chain of command. If you look at the organogram drafted by General Petkovic's Defence, then you see that it shows the various organs or, rather, bodies of Herceg-Bosna which were tasked in certain aspects with the issues of defence. It is drafted based on the Decree on the Armed Forces. This was prescribed by regulation in Herceg-Bosna. I don't think these two organograms can be compared at all or that one can be rejected in favour of another. They simply serve a different function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What matters is what General Praljak thinks of the organisation charts. And the second one, do you agree with the second organisation chart, or do you have any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, it is precisely what was said. When we need a car or equipment or something, then I or my assistant turned to Bruno Stojic. But when I was supposed to deal with the chain of command, I didn't deal with Mr. Stojic, but with Mr. Boban. The Main Staff was within the Defence Department, of course, and it relied on it in various matters such as healthcare, but in terms of functionality, Bruno Stojic was not my superior, he did not command me. One cannot simplify it then to say one thing or the other. For each thing, we need to ascertain who was competent for what. For example, if one needed a pair of shoes, then it's Bruno Stojic. When I needed to check whether an order is fine, then I had to go to Mate Boban. So it's both, but one thing is in terms of function and operational use, such as with the military police; for example, who was in charge of personnel, who was in charge of promotion, commendations, et cetera. It's all separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We need to have a break now - we are running a few minutes late - and we shall resume afterwards. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session, and, Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, staying with this Exhibit 4D01280, 1280, one last question or so about it. If we look at this in the colour version, the middle section, which is the Defence Department, which is itself a part of the Government of the HZ-HB, and then moving down, actually, to the bottom, where we have the Armed Forces of the HZ-HB, would you agree with me that this is an accurate -- this chart is accurate, in that it indicates or suggests that all of these various departments or, I should say, sectors, as well as the Main Staff, all of these branches of the Defence Department basically exist in order to administer or to regulate or to ensure the effective operations of the armed forces, they all have that function which in some way relates to running or supporting the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Department of Defence was there precisely for defence, but "defence" is a much broader term than the armed forces themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think an over-simplification does not amount to anything good. I really don't know how to answer this, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll put it to you this way: that each of these branches of the Defence Department had a role to play in the operation of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was their function, to assist the armed forces, that is correct. However, the armed forces is not only the army. The armed forces are a broader term than the HVO itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, on that, I mean, when we talk about the armed forces, what's indicated here are commands, operative zone -- well, strike that. Actually, we'll probably talk about that more when we look at the Decree on the Armed Forces, so I think we can just leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Praljak, on this same chart we find, in the yellow sector, with the government and the ministry, in the Security Sector, reference to Military Police Administration and head of Military Police, whereas the Military Police itself we find in the blue sector that is the Armed Forces sector. Could you explain how come that the Command and Administration of the Military Police are, according to this diagram, always placed within the Department of Defence, which basically is a civilian organisation, whereas the Military Police itself is separated and figures with the Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I don't see that. Where do you find that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you take the yellow sector, you have first the Department of Defence. Then you have two lines, the first giving the title of the separate sectors. Then in the next line there's just the word "assistants" four times. It doesn't figure in the first chapter. And then in the Security Sector, which is the second column from the left, you have a separation in two columns. One is the SIS, and the other says "MP Military Police Admin," administration, and "head of Military Police." But then if you go to the blue sector, the second line here, the second department -- there we find "Military Police." In other words, we have the Administration and the head of the Military Police in this civil body, but the Military Police itself in the military, and I find it a bit puzzling. And if you can, I would be grateful for an explanation. If you cannot, that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Croatian Army, and this should have been the same, there should have been an assistant for security. Then that assistant administered both the SIS and the Military Police, because one body is in charge of detecting crime and the other one of submitting criminal reports, investigating. They share the same technical base for research and investigation in order to gather evidence. However, all those within the structure, including the Civilian Protection and so on, can at a certain moment represent something that is generally known as the armed forces. It is the HVO and all those bearing arms. If there is such a situation which general defence is required, then, for example, in my case I was allowed to use the military police for operational purposes as well. That doesn't mean that it came outside its structure in terms of supplies, personnel policy, disciplining, et cetera. I believe this is the same in other armed forces of the world and in other civil states. One body provides for the budget and administrates, and the other body dictates the use of such units prescribed under the law. I don't see, Your Honour, anything wrong there. The military police is, with the armed forces, taking care of security, traffic safety, and everything they had to do, but once there was an all-out attack, then the military police could be used, by virtue of a decision, could be attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is repetitious. I simply find it a bit strange that the head of the Military Police is in one corner and the Military Police, itself, is in the other one. But you have commented on this, the administration, and that I have no problems with at all, but I think I leave it at that. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit that I'd like to take us to is P00965. This document is from the 31st of December, 1992, so it's before the time that you became commander of the Main Staff, but it's during the period of time that you were involved with certain HVO commands and activities. It is a report from Mr. Primorac, Ivica Primorac, on the situation in the professional structure of the HVO. It's directed to the head of the Defence Department, Bruno Stojic, and also to Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, who was the commander of the HVO at that time. And it states that the following form a part of units in the professional structure of the HVO. And then right off the bat it starts with the professional units we've talked about already, which is the Bruno Busic unit and the Ludvig Pavlovic special-purpose unit. And my question is, General: You've indicated that at least from the 24 July, 1993, these two units were directly subordinated to or within the structure of the Main Staff. Do you know whether these units were in the Main Staff structure during this period of time, December 1992? Were they a part of the Main Staff or did they fall somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said something to the extent that I was busy with some of these things, whereas I wasn't. I can't answer this question of yours. I don't know. This document is something I see for the first time, and I can't say anything about it. I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, in October of 1992, when the events occurred in Prozor, where you were present and were commanding, in a de facto capacity, HVO personnel and units, do you know whether in October of 1992 the Bruno Busic Regiment or the Ludvig Pavlovic Special Unit were -- formed part of the structure of the Main Staff, or were they more linked closely -- more closely linked to the Defence Department, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, first you state something like "when you were in Prozor, commanding," so you're not asking me but stating something, and then you move on and put the question at the end. And when I say "yes" or "no," I am supposed to include all of your question/statement in my answer. Please state a question and leave the comments for some other time. If you're asking me whether I commanded and then everything that followed, then I'll simply ask you to break down these lengthy explications that you are seeking answers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In October of 1992, at the time of the events in Prozor, do you know whether the Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic units were attached to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were attached to the Main Staff in December of 1992, 31 December, the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, General, that you only know that from 24 July 1993, these two units were attached to the Main Staff, as you've already testified?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state that with certainty. The rest would be speculation which may or may not be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you'll turn the page, actually, turning the page in the English version, there are four more units that are referred to here: The Vitezovi, the Baja Kraljevic ATG, Convicts Battalion, commanded by Mario Hrkac, and the Tvrtko II. Now, let's talk about the period of time after the 24th of July, 1993. General, do you know whether these units were attached to -- directly subordinated to the Main Staff, of which you were the commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I commanded the Ludvig Pavlovic and Bruno Busic units. As for Vitezovi, I don't know what was going on up there. Blaskic asked for assistance concerning this Darko [as interpreted] Kraljevic. As for this Tvrtko unit, this is the first time I hear about it. I did not command the Convicts Battalion, but I did command the unit called Baja Kraljevic which was in charge of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name of the commander of that unit. Could the witness please repeat the end of the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were just talking about the Baja Kraljevic ATG unit, General. Is that the unit that was commanded by Predrag Mandic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably know that Predrag Mandic commanded a unit, and I do know that, as far as I know, that he was a good soldier and he carried out orders. Probably the unit was called Baja Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Baja Kraljevic ATG, then, during the period after you became the commander of the HVO, are you saying that that is a unit that is like Bruno Busic, that was always directly a part of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question completely, to tell you the truth. There was such a unit, the commander of which was Predrag Mandic. As for the structure and whether it shared the status of the Bruno Busic or the other unit, I don't know. It was a smaller unit with -- whose structure I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, you just told us that you did command the Baja Kraljevic unit, so are you telling us that that's because it was directly subordinated to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I could command the unit that Predrag Mandic was in charge of. They did obey, that is correct. But I had no time, save for the two units, I had no time to ascertain who was subordinated to the Main Staff and who was not. It was such a war in which I had no time for that. I can only tell you that Predrag Mandic carried out orders. As for the exact name of that unit, I don't know. Well, I guess it was the Baja Kraljevic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, what I'm getting at is this: If we go back to the chart from your testimony in the Tuta Stela case, which is our Exhibit P09324, this one [indicates], in your handwriting you put this "ATG" letters and you, with the arrow, are putting the "ATG" into the box for these professional units and units for special assignments, and you're doing that on this chart that you've approved or that you've written on, which directly links those particular units to the Defence Department. So I'm asking whether, in fact, the Baja Kraljevic was -- because it was an ATG, was a part of the or linked directly to the Defence Department, but that it could be deployed by the Main Staff if the necessary arrangements and coordination took place with the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I told you precisely. The unit commanded by Predrag Mandic was a unit that I could issue orders to. I can't tell you anything more, for the simple reason that I was not familiar with the things as they were on paper. The war had begun. We had a large offensive of the Muslim forces along a 200-kilometre line, and I had to come up with people who would carry out my orders without fleeing. That's it, to put things short.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, then, if I understand correctly what you're saying, the Baja Kraljevic unit, which you commanded at the time you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, is a unit which you don't know where it would fit within this diagram; is that how it goes? You don't know whether it goes down here under the Main Staff or you don't know whether it fits out here with the special units; all you know is that you commanded them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It carried out orders. If one sent an order, the commander would implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go a bit farther into this document. But continuing on, this indicates that at the time this document was written, the Bruno Busic Regiment was in the process of relocating to the Heliodrom. I'm going to skip over a couple of these other units that we haven't talked about, but others are being relocated to the Heliodrom as well. And then turning the page in the English, I want to go to the Ludvig Pavlovic Special Purpose Unit. It says: "Ludvig Pavlovic Special Purpose Unit, Capljina, has a completely professional attitude toward all assigned tasks. It is well equipped materially and well trained. Its relocation from the Gabela Barracks to the Bozan Simovic Barracks of Grabovina has ensured the conditions for this unit which is organised militarily in excellent fashion to be reinforced and to become a formation of battalion strength." So is that an accurate statement, based on what you -- let me put it this way: Did you know anything about the Ludvig Pavlovic unit before you took command of the HVO Main Staff in July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, tell us, what did you know about them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first time I encountered the Ludvig Pavlovic unit while Bozan Simovic was its commander. He was killed in 1992, during an operation in which the HVO was pushing the Serbs back in October 1992. I think it was called Operation Bura. I was very familiar with their commander, who is today a general, Dragan Curcic. I fought alongside them in Capljina against Republika Srpska. It has always been an excellent unit, well organised, well behaved, and they acted professionally. At this point in time, they comprised several hundred men. They were at the level of battalion. As for their commanders, military discipline, executing orders, and courage, as well as the number of losses they sustained, based on all that, one can say all the best about that unit. I also fought alongside them at Boksavica and later --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. When you were fighting along them in Boksavica, now, are you talking about the period of June and early July 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: End June, early July, yes, and in some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is shortly before you took command of the HVO Main Staff. Do you know whether, at Boksavica, this unit was attached directly to the Main Staff or whether, as a professional unit, it was more directly linked to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We were together up there. As for the basis for of their presence there, I don't know. A smaller part of that unit was there, including Mr. Curcic. They sustained losses. Some of their men were captured. This unit was at first called "Krajl Tomislav," and at first it was under Mr. Izetbegovic. And then when it was under Mr. Daidza, a lot of Muslims went through that unit who later joined the Army of B and H. An excellent unit, excellent commanders, completely professional in the military sense and moral in every aspect. The same goes for the Bruno Busic unit, which was later under Mr. Luburic, whom I had brought from Vukovar as a volunteer. He arrived there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So as to Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic, then, just to finish those off, what we can say with certainty is that those two units were directly subordinated to the HVO Main Staff during the period that you were the commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I commanded the Main Staff, they were subordinated to me, and I could direct them, in the military sense. I don't know anything about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next unit that's referred to here, Convicts Battalion, Mostar, Heliodrom. During the time that you commanded the HVO Main Staff, was that unit directly subordinated to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There was a unit which was under the command of Mr. Andabak, and there was some contentious names there. Now, I met Mr. Andabak in 1992, in Capljina, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's all right, General. I'm not going to ask you about that. If you don't know if the Convicts Battalion, Mostar, was attached to the Main Staff, do you know if it fell within the group of units that was attached or linked to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Same question about Baja Kraljevic Anti-Terrorist Group, Mostar. Main Staff, or Defence Department, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I asked Mandic to go to the front to fight, he obeyed, and that's a fact. Now, what belonged to whom, I didn't have time to investigate things like that. I wasn't interested. I was just interested in knowing which units and commanders were capable of carrying out an order and in what way, and I can give you a precise answer to things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, then, did they have the same status as the Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't think so. I don't know. The correct answer would be I don't know, but -- well, I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, the next thing -- unless there's any questions on this document, I'm going to move to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, let me come back to the anti-terrorist group, the Baja Kraljevic Anti-Terrorist Group. It seems a bit fuzzy, all this. The Prosecutor is asking you whether this group is attached to the Department of Defence, and you can't answer, so let's assume -- let's assume two things. First assumption: It is attached to the Department of Defence, which means that Mr. Stojic is on the front-line here, he's the one in charge of deciding to send this ATG on different locations. Second assumption: This group is not subordinated to the DOD, but falls within the Main Staff. When you took command in July, did this anti-terrorist -- did you have to give any orders to this anti-terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember that I issued direct orders to Baja Kraljevic. It was too small a unit, and probably that went via -- well, I don't know. Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, let's be quite clear. I don't know whether somebody else could have commanded that unit. That's what I don't know. I know what I do know, that I would see Mr. Mandic, and his nickname was Lija, and that dates back to the Prozor days and my days in Konjic and Jablanica and so on, and he listened to the oral order and acted upon it. Now, whether he carried out somebody else's order, I can't know that. Anyway, Ludvig Pavlovic, Bruno Busic, and Baja Kraljevic, I could issue orders to those men, and those commanders, Curcic, Luburic, Mandic, would carry them out, and as far as I know, they were good units. That's what I know. Now, as to all the rest of it, whether somebody else could issue orders, whether there were more of them, I don't know that, I can't know that, nor did I have time to inquire and investigate it. It was -- we had a war on for three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I believe you've answered this already. We would have to leaf through these thousands of pages of the transcript, and so let's go straight to the point. An anti-terrorist group, well, what was its main purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, these people quite simply wanted to be called by some special name, probably having watched too many movies or whatever. Anyway, they were just people who were a little better fighters than the ones who were mobilised, so if they need -- when the lines fell, for example, if there was a breakthrough in the lines and we had to stop that onslaught and retake control of the lines again, then you would call in one of these units. Now, what they were called, ATGs, anti-terrorist, blah-blah-blah, or whatever, it doesn't matter, it's immaterial. But, anyway, they were people who were chosen as being better fighters. So whether you needed to take back control of the lines or take some feature and elevation, you would solve that problem with them, you would do so with them, because they were better than the rest, better than the other units that had been mobilised 10 or 15 days before that and stood guard at the line, and very often they would lose the line, lose a battle, and then you would have to use better units to regain control; that's as far as the war goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, actually, I'm going to stay with this for just a couple more minutes and ask you an open-ended question. Back to P09324, which is the chart that you were marking on when you testified in the Tuta Stela case, here, for the box on the right, which is for units -- for special assignments and professional units, you wrote "ATG" and you pointed an arrow pointed at that box. Can you tell us what ATG units you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's what I'm telling you today, and I'm saying that these three units -- I'm telling you very precisely about how it was when I was in command of the Main Staff, who, in the military sense, I could rely on most in critical situations on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm actually -- I'm asking you a different question, because we're looking at a box here that's linked directly to the Defence Department and not to the Main Staff. It's a chart that you accepted as more or less accurate when you testified, so I'm asking you: When you wrote the "ATG" here and you made -- and you pointed the arrow at the box on professional and special units, what -- can you name the ATG units that you are linking to this box on special units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, if you skip my introductory sentence which says, in response to that question, that I don't know about this with any certainty, so if you skip that sentence, then, of course, you follow along your argument, and this lack of security on my part, in my knowledge, you want to turn that into something else. I drew this along with the sentence that I stated at the very beginning, with caveats and provisos, and I'm going to explain them. And I mentioned three units with which I, when I was commander, was able to command, and that's all. That's all I have to say. So try -- don't try and read more into it than I'm telling you. Read the first sentence, then go on with your questions. So along with that caveat, but it -- so I have to use that caveat, and I say "ATG," Baja Kraljevic, commander Predrag Mandic, for example, he was a good commander. That's a small unit, and he would have obeyed an oral order given. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, here, on the other side of this box on professional and special units, you wrote "KB," which stands for "Kaznjenicka Bojna," which is the Convicts Battalion, so is it correct, General, that the Convicts Battalion belongs in this box on professional and special units? That's what you said under oath back in April of 2002, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote "KB," that is to say, Convicts Battalion. You don't have to remind me that I said this on oath. I also stipulated my caveat on oath, that my knowledge is not certain. So that sentence was uttered under oath, too. Now, the unit commanded by Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was not one that was under my command. There you have it. Now, as to the Predrag Mandic unit, whatever its name was, and I'm not sure of what that was, I could have commanded that, and that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to your testimony from Tuta Stela, page 98 -- I'm sorry, page 9580, beginning on line 9. I'll read the question, and this is on cross-examination from Mr. Scott, and he says -- we can put this up in Sanction on the screen, if anybody wants to follow it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But could I have the Croatian in front of me so that I can read through it to look at all the nuances of what was said? I think that would be in order, that you give me a copy of the document that you're referring to in the Croatian original, and I think that is your duty. It is your duty to provide me with that text so that I can see all the shades of meaning, because otherwise I'm in a second-rate position because I can't refer to the second sentence, which is the key to understanding all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have transcripts in your language of your testimony at proceedings at the Tribunal, and so we have to work as best we can. So I've put it up in English, which I know doesn't assist you very much, but your counsel can follow along, and I'm just going to read this part to you and you can comment on it, and I'm sure the Judges will take into account the fact that you don't have it in your own language. The question from Mr. Scott is this. He says: "You testified a few moments ago that Bruno Stojic was the head of the Defence Department. Now, does this chart indicate -- could he call up and issue commands to a professional unit without going to the Main Staff?" And this is your answer. You say: "Well, he could have done it, but it was usually done by agreement. He could not command that unit once it had arrived at the front-line - defence line, excuse me - with somebody because of poor communications or because I was too far away, because Mr. Petkovic was somewhere far away, that Mr. Tole was somewhere on the ground, and the situation made it imperative. Then it would -- then one could go through Mr. Stojic to ask him to send a unit. But once that unit arrived at the front, it would become a part of the structure commanded by somebody from the Operative Zone or that front-line to which they had come, more narrowly speaking." So, General, is that more or less an accurate statement of how it worked, and that Mr. Stojic did have the ability or the authority to order units to go somewhere if the situation required it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described exactly under what circumstances this was, so it wasn't a situation when I could come into contact only with Bruno Stojic and Petkovic was in Central Bosnia or whatever, and I couldn't contact the Main Staff, for example. Then I could ask him to issue an order to Ludvig Pavlovic to set out somewhere, to go somewhere. That's bypassing the system. So I'm talking about the time I was there. In a special situation during a war, where you have very poor communications, where the front is a long one, and where our defence forces have been stretched out, stretched to the limits, and a weak -- the party attacking is strong, the offensive has been going on for months, then the variants that I stipulate here are possible, they are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let me ask it this way. I'm having trouble getting something that I can understand, and I don't know whether it's my fault or yours. I think we -- let's start with the military police. Can we agree that apart from this situation that related to Operation Buna, that the normal procedure was that if an operative zone needed a military police battalion to be deployed for operational purposes, it had to get the permission of Bruno Stojic to do that? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can. So the military police was not -- which is why I asked permission. The military police was not under the command of the Main Staff up until the point until this was settled in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then the question becomes: Were there other units that fell under that same category, whether we call them ATGs or special-purpose units or professional units? Were there any other units that the Main Staff had to go to Mr. Stojic for -- about before those units could be deployed into an operative zone structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was commander, I didn't ask for any permission like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So the answer is you don't know; is that a correct way to frame your answer, that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't understand my answer in any other way except in the way I said it. During the time I was in command, I would issue a direct order to the Ludvig Pavlovic unit if I was able to come in to contact with it. If I was not able to communicate with them for any reason, and there were many reasons why not, then I could have conveyed this and said, Mr. Stringer, would you convey a message to Mrs. Pinter, for example, to tell Pavlovic to get out of bed straight away because such and such had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, General, a different question. We've agreed on what the situation was with military police units. I'm simply asking you whether the same situation applied to any other units that you're aware of.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I give you an answer, that answer would not be correct, because I can't answer the question because I don't know. I claim that during the time that I was in command, I could -- and don't let's go back to that question. I'm going to repeat this ten times, and you're going to try and make something of me that you will never succeed in doing. You will never get me to give you erroneous information or information that I'm not sure about. So my answer is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm finished with this line, and it probably would be best to finish today before I open a new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. I had just one follow-up question, which is a very brief question. When you testified in the Naletilic case, a question was put to you on the word "ATG." You answered by saying: "I know what this means." And you explained that when the ATGs met on the front-line, they were then placed under the command of the commander of that zone on the front-line. Does this mean that whatever the status of these professional units was, when these are placed in a combat zone they are automatically placed under the command of the person exercising military authority in the combat zone? Can you answer the question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. If it arrived in a regular way, it was under that command, but they might come and go according to how they wanted to. They weren't under my command or the operative command, and I didn't know whose command they were under. If you see people coming and going whenever they felt like it, and you saw these examples, all you can do is write up a report, and that's where it all ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am sure we will have the opportunity to get back to these questions in the next few days. The court stands adjourned, since I have another hearing in another case, and we shall meet tomorrow at 9.00.
